summary: This version of the Restaurant class adds a placeOrder method that refuses orders before 11:00 AM. Instead of asking the system for the time directly, it reads the time through a Clock object that is handed in when the restaurant is created, which is what lets a test pretend it is any hour of the day.

lines.text: Clock is Java's replaceable source of the current time; importing it is the first step toward making time testable rather than fixed.

lines.code: private static final LocalTime ORDER_OPEN_TIME = LocalTime.of(11, 0);
lines.text: The opening time is a named constant, so the rule "orders open at 11:00" lives in one place instead of being buried in the comparison below.
Each Restaurant keeps its own clock, and marking it final guarantees nothing can swap the clock out after construction.
The no-argument constructor keeps ordinary use simple: callers who do not care about time can still write new Restaurant().
This delegates to the other constructor, supplying the real system clock as the default so production code behaves normally.
This second constructor is the seam a test uses, because it accepts any clock, including a fixed one frozen at a chosen hour.
A placeholder marking where the spice level method from the earlier exercise still belongs; the listing omits it to keep the focus on ordering.
Returning a String rather than printing means a test can compare the result directly, with no need to capture console output.
Asking LocalTime.now for the time held by this clock is the key move: with a fixed clock the method sees whatever time the test chose.
isBefore compares the two times, so anything earlier than 11:00 falls into the rejection branch.
Returning early stops the order from being placed and tells the caller why.
Reaching this line means the time is 11:00 or later, so the order is accepted and echoed back with the item name.
